title: Jim Coplien and Bob Martin Debate TDD
summary: Coplien and Martin debate whether TDD is a professional obligation and whether driving architecture from unit tests damages design.

assertions.quote: it is irresponsible for a developer to ship a line of code that he has not executed in unit test

verdicts.note: A professional norm rather than a measurable outcome; whether untested code ships is checkable, whether that is unprofessional is a value judgment.

Authors concede that following the test-first rule prevents shortcuts that skip tests, but an ethnographic study found developers wrote more production code than needed, omitted refactoring and let tests fall behind even when nominally test-first; the 'unprofessional' judgment is not testable.

assertions.quote: leads to a procedural bottomup architecture because the things you're testing are units

verdicts.note: Design damage from test-driven isolation is reported in case studies and the DHH debate, but controlled studies of TDD's design effects are mixed and small.

assertions.quote: the architecture evolves it is informed by code that executes and it is informed by the test that you write

verdicts.note: Incremental architecture is standard agile practice, but there is no controlled evidence it beats moderate up-front design and both debaters endorse some up-front structure.

The review reports lack of attention to design and architectural issues as a limitation found in an agile study and repeatedly raised in the literature, so incremental evolution carries a documented risk of under-investing in architecture; the studies are weak and do not test the claim directly.

assertions.quote: you're not going to refactor your way to the right architecture from from that one

verdicts.note: Large-scale architectural decisions are known to be costly to reverse, but how much up-front design is needed is unresolved.

Participants in an XP project said there were not enough discussions on design and architecture, and the review lists lack of attention to architecture as a recurring limitation of agile development; this supports the worry but not the specific claim that incremental refactoring cannot reach the right architecture.

assertions.quote: they actually give you broader coverage because you're covering the entire range of the arguments rather than just you know randomly scattering some values

verdicts.note: Contracts specify behaviour over all inputs but are only enforced on executed inputs unless statically verified, so coverage gains depend on tooling.

assertions.quote: the code mass is is about the same as a test mass and whereas there's code there's bugs you cut your velocity in half
it's really really difficult to trace those those apis at a class level sometimes all the way up to business significance

verdicts.note: A judgment about traceability rather than a measurable claim.
